To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
motor performance is modulated by a monetary incentive and that the sensitivity to incentive depends on individual characteristics of the subjects.
motor performance is influenced by the amount of monetary reward and the average reward experienced during a previous task.
motor performance increases with the amount and with the average value of a monetary incentive.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how motor performance is influenced by a monetary incentive.
the mechanisms underlying the control of movement and the selection of motor actions.
the study of the relationship between motor performance and the perceived benefits of successful movement completion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
motor performance is a function of the perceived incentive, and that the perceived incentive is in turn a function of the average reward.
the trade-off between accuracy and energetic expenditure depends on the subjective value of the task.
motor performance increases with the perceived benefits associated to successful movement, and the way these benefits are perceived is subject-dependent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
motor performance can be modulated by monetary incentive and that this effect is subject-specific.
the sensitivity to incentive and the sensitivity to reward are inversely correlated.
motor performance is a complex function of the task, the incentive and the subject.
The main takeaway from our work is that

motor performance is not just a consequence of movement accuracy and energetic cost but also of the perceived benefit associated with the task completion, and that these factors may be modulated by a monetary incentive.
the trade-off between accuracy and energetic costs is modulated by the perceived benefit associated to the movement completion.
the trade-off between accuracy and energy expenditure in motor behavior is not a fixed property but rather depends on the perceived benefits (and costs) associated to successful performance.
